quick.summary: Why saving the code is only half the job, and where the rest goes.
quick.takeaway: Update the documentation at the exact same time you update the code.

parts.title: Write down what data means

beats.line: I spent three hours guessing what the status column means. Why is this hidden?
It was put in a blank jar. You need a label.
Like a label in a pantry saying if it is flour or sugar.
Exactly. We call that label semantic metadata.
Can I just say data context?
Yes. Context is exactly what we need.
Context tells us where the numbers came from and what they really measure.
So I should write down if status means paid or just shipped.
But where do I actually write this down so people find it?

parts.cliff: Where do we actually put these labels?

beats.line: We keep these labels in a central list, like a public library catalog.
So anyone in the company can look up the table and read the meaning.
Yes. But a list is useless if the books are never updated.
Right. When a column changes, the old context is basically a lie.
Exactly. Documentation is part of the code, not an afterthought.
Whenever you change a pipeline, you update the description at the same time.
So I treat updates to the code and the context as one single task.
Exactly. You leave the labels accurate for the next person.

quiz.question: Why do we need context written down for our data?
options: So the next person knows what it really measures.
So the pipeline runs smoothly without errors.
So the data takes up less storage space.
So the tables look professional to clients.
quiz.explanation: Context explains the meaning of data, stopping others from guessing and making mistakes.

quiz.question: You should update the data documentation only when you have free time.
quiz.explanation: Documentation should be updated at the same time you change the code, so it is never out of date.
